title: True-PolyTronik: Securing Circuits Against Laser Logic State Imaging Attack Using RFET
problem: Optical Probing (OP) with Laser Logic State Imaging (LLSI) attack can extract static transistor state from SRAM, combinational circuits, and sequential logic by modulating power supply at low frequency/amplitude. Existing mitigation techniques are power-hungry, require large supply modulation, or need costly laser sensors.
motivation: LLSI attacks pose serious threat to chip security, especially for sensitive data (keys, intermediate values, secrets). Existing defenses lack practical deployment path due to high overhead or invasive modifications. Integration with standard CMOS fabrication is essential.
method: Uses reconfigurable transistors (RFETs—transistors that can be switched between positive-channel and negative-channel types) embedded in logic cells designed to sense small ripples in the power supply. Upon detecting an LLSI attack, the RFETs automatically corrupt the circuit's internal state by applying a biased voltage to their control pins, scrambling the data an attacker is trying to read via optical imaging. A biasing circuit holds these control pins at a steady voltage during the attack to ensure reliable state destruction. The approach was tested on combinational logic and D-latch cells.
key_novelty: First defense against LLSI attacks using RFET transistors, which reconfigure themselves during an attack to automatically destroy stored state, eliminating the need for external laser sensors or large power-supply changes.
contributions: RFET-based logic cells capable of detecting small power supply modulation
Runtime reconfiguration for corrupting static state upon LLSI attack
Program pin biasing circuitry generating stable voltage during attack
Compatibility with CMOS fabrication (RFET integrates seamlessly)
Demonstration on combinational logic and D-latch cells
Performance comparison: protected vs. unprotected implementations
limitations: RFET technology availability and maturity not discussed
Area overhead for RFET-based protection not provided
Limited attack model: assumes low-frequency power modulation only; multi-frequency or different OP techniques not addressed
No formal security proof or threat model rigor
Scalability to full SoC protection not demonstrated; only logic cells shown
Side-channel vulnerability of program pin circuitry not analyzed
Cost comparison vs. existing defenses (sensors, special devices) not provided
